cards.prose: The council that met at daybreak to put Yahusha (Jesus) to death is the same company that ends up holding thirty pieces of silver. In Zechariah the shepherd asks for his wages and is weighed exactly that sum, and the next line tells him where to throw it: *Cast it unto the potter* (Zechariah 11:13). It is the price put on the shepherd of the flock.
cards.member_phrase: So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver.
cards.member_sentence: The shepherd is paid thirty pieces of silver for his work, the sum later weighed out as the price on Yahusha (Jesus).
cards.flag: The card hangs on 27:1, but its point sits in the Judas verses a few lines on; the prose bridges by the council.

cards.prose: The same two groups meet in both places, the elders of the people and the elders of the priests. Yahuah (the LORD) sends Jeremiah to them with a potter's earthen bottle and a charge, that they had *filled this place with the blood of innocents* (Jeremiah 19:4). Matthew names Jeremiah over the potter's field, and this is the chapter where the potter and the blood stand together.
cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.member_sentence: Jeremiah takes a potter's bottle to the elders and priests in the valley of Hinnom, where the charge is innocent blood.

cards.prose: Matthew names Jeremiah over the field the priests bought, and this is the chapter where Jeremiah buys a field. He does it at the word of Yahuah (the LORD), when his uncle's son offers it, and in his own words he *weighed him the money, even seventeen shekels of silver* (Jeremiah 32:9). A field bought with weighed silver is the thread that runs between the two stories.
cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.member_sentence: Jeremiah buys a field at the word of Yahuah (the LORD) and weighs out silver for it, the other field behind the potter's field.

cards.prose: This is David's verse about the man set against him, and Peter later takes it for Judas, who sat among the twelve. The council that morning needed one of the twelve to hand Yahusha (Jesus) over, and the verse says what happens to the office he leaves: another takes it.
cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.member_sentence: David asks that another take the office of the man who turns on him, the verse Peter later reads over Judas.

cards.prose: Peter says the scripture had to be fulfilled, spoken by the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit) through David *concerning Judas, which was guide to them that took Yahusha (Jesus)*. The chief priests and elders taking counsel in Matthew are the ones he guided them to. Judas was not a stranger to the work; he stood among the twelve.
cards.member_phrase: which the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit) by the mouth of David spake before concerning Judas
cards.member_sentence: Peter tells the disciples that David spoke by the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit) about Judas, who guided those who took Yahusha (Jesus).

cards.prose: Later that morning the silver comes back to those same priests, and they will not put it in the treasury because it is the price of blood. The commandment behind their words keeps such money out of the house of Yahuah (the LORD). The Torah is right in this; it is the court that is wrong, for it kept the line carefully while the man the money paid for was being handed over.
cards.member_phrase: Thou shalt not bring the hire of a whore, or the price of a dog, into the house of Yahuah Elohayka (the LORD thy God)
cards.member_sentence: The Torah keeps the hire of a whore and the price of a dog out of the house of Yahuah (the LORD), the line the priests lean on.
cards.flag: Same as the others in this group: the card sits on 27:1 but is about the silver, three verses on.

cards.prose: Mark says who stood behind the hand-over: the chief priests with the elders and scribes and *the whole council* bound Yahusha (Jesus) and carried him to Pilate. When the governor asks if he is the King of the Yahudim (Jews), the question has been brought to him by the court and not made up in the room.
cards.member_phrase: the chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council
cards.member_sentence: Mark has the whole council bind Yahusha (Jesus) in the morning and hand him to Pilate.

cards.prose: Luke has them all rise and lead him to Pilate, and then he names the charge: *forbidding to give tribute to Cæsar, saying that he himself is Messiah (Christ) a King* (Luke 23:2). That is why Pilate asks the question he does in Matthew, and Yahusha's (Jesus's) answer is the same, *Thou sayest*. Luke goes on to a hearing before Herod that Matthew leaves out.
cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.member_sentence: Luke has the whole company lead Yahusha (Jesus) to Pilate and gives the charge that stands behind the governor's question.

cards.prose: John shows the rulers standing outside the governor's hall so as not to be defiled, because they meant to *eat the passover*. They had put an innocent man before a Roman and were careful about the cleanness of the feast. Nobody in the verse argues the Passover away; what is on trial is a court that kept the feast with one hand and handed Yahusha (Jesus) over with the other.
cards.member_phrase: they themselves went not into the judgment hall, lest they should be defiled; but that they might eat the passover.
cards.member_sentence: The rulers who bring Yahusha (Jesus) to Pilate will not enter his hall, lest they be defiled before they eat the passover.

cards.prose: Yahusha (Jesus) says *Thou sayest* to the question about a king, and when the chief priests and elders press their charges Matthew says *he answered nothing* (Matthew 27:12). Isaiah's servant is the same: afflicted, yet *he openeth not his mouth*, like a lamb brought to the slaughter. He answers what is true and lets the accusations go by.
cards.member_phrase: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb
cards.member_sentence: Isaiah's servant is afflicted and silent as a lamb before the slaughter, the silence Pilate marvels at.

cards.prose: Pilate washes his hands later in this same hearing, and he is borrowing a ceremony Moses gave. When a slain man is found and no one knows who killed him, the elders of the nearest city come forward and clear themselves. That ceremony is for blood whose killer is unknown. Matthew says Pilate knew it was envy that had delivered Yahusha (Jesus) up, so he took the gesture without the case it was made for.
cards.member_phrase: and it be not known who hath slain him
cards.member_sentence: Deuteronomy 21 gives the elders' cleansing for a killing no one can name, the ceremony Pilate's hand-washing borrows.
cards.flag: The pair is pinned to 27:11, but it belongs to Pilate's hand-washing at 27:24-25, so I put it in the 27:25 thread; the prose tells the reader that.

cards.prose: Peter's account agrees with Matthew's: Pilate *was determined to let him go*, and the delivering up and the denial came from those who pressed him. Peter calls Yahusha (Jesus) the Son whom the Elohim (God) of Abraham, of Isaac and of Jacob has glorified, so the one standing before the governor already belonged to the fathers.
cards.member_phrase: hath glorified his Son Yahusha (Jesus); whom ye delivered up, and denied him in the presence of Pilate, when he was determined to let him go
cards.member_sentence: Peter says the Elohim (God) of the fathers glorified Yahusha (Jesus), and that Pilate was determined to release him.
cards.flag: Acts 3:13 is spoken to men of Yashar'el (Israel); I wrote it so the charge rests on those who pressed the delivering up (the rulers, 27:20), not on a people.

cards.prose: The believers in Acts pray David's psalm over this very trial. They name the kings and rulers gathered *against Yahuah (Lord), and against his Messiah (Christ)* (Acts 4:26), and then Herod, Pilate, the nations and the people together. In Matthew the chief priests, the elders and the governor are those rulers, and the one in front of the governor is the anointed.
cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.member_sentence: The believers pray David's psalm about the rulers raging against the anointed, naming the gathering that stood before Pilate.
cards.flag: Placed in the 27:25 thread because it names the rulers' gathering, and the people stirred by them; it could also sit with the Pilate scene.

cards.prose: Mark names the hall, the Prætorium, where Matthew says only the common hall, and his *whole band* is the same company of soldiers gathered to mock one man. He then lists the purple, the crown of thorns and the salute, so the two accounts tell one scene, each with the blows set down plainly.
cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.member_sentence: Mark names the hall as the Prætorium and has the soldiers call together the whole band.

cards.prose: Luke names the man the soldiers seized on the road: Simon, a Cyrenian, coming in from the country, who was made to carry the cross *after Yahusha (Jesus)*. Matthew's soldiers have just finished their sport in the hall, and Luke shows what the way out looked like, with a stranger pressed into service and a great company, women among them, following behind.
cards.member_phrase: they laid hold upon one Simon, a Cyrenian, coming out of the country, and on him they laid the cross
cards.member_sentence: Luke names Simon the Cyrenian as the man made to carry the cross after Yahusha (Jesus).

cards.prose: John says he went out *bearing his cross* to the place of a skull, called in Hebrew Golgotha, where Matthew's soldiers take him once the robe is off. John tells that he began by bearing it himself and Matthew that Simon was found along the way, and both end the road at Golgotha.
cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.member_sentence: John has Yahusha (Jesus) go out bearing his cross to Golgotha, the place of a skull.

cards.prose: In the hall the soldiers strike him and spit on him. Isaiah's servant speaks of just that: *I gave my back to the smiters*, he says, and *hid not my face from shame and spitting*. His word is *gave*, and it matches one who is not being dragged but is giving, the way Yahusha (Jesus) went through that hall.
cards.member_phrase: I hid not my face from shame and spitting
cards.member_sentence: The servant gives his back to the smiters and does not hide his face from shame and spitting.

cards.prose: The soldiers bow before a man they take for nobody. Isaiah says of the servant that he is *despised and rejected of men*, and that men *hid as it were our faces from him*. He is also *a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief*, and the hall shows how little the men in it thought of him.
cards.member_phrase: He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief
cards.member_sentence: The servant is despised and rejected, a man of sorrows whom men would not look at.

cards.prose: Through the robe, the reed and the blows, Matthew gives Yahusha (Jesus) no word to say. Isaiah has the same silence: oppressed and afflicted, *yet he opened not his mouth*. The hall is the second place after Pilate's where that silence is tested, and it holds.
cards.member_phrase: He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth
cards.member_sentence: The servant is oppressed and afflicted and opens not his mouth, the silence held through the soldiers' sport.

cards.prose: David's psalm has the watchers laughing, shooting out the lip and shaking the head, and then it gives them words to say. All of it is around the cross: the soldiers laugh in the hall, the passers-by wag their heads, and the rulers say what the psalm already had in their mouths. David wrote the scene long before, from the inside.
cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.member_sentence: David's psalm has the onlookers laugh him to scorn and shake the head, as the crowd does at the cross.

cards.prose: The whole band gathered around one man in the hall reads like David's picture: *dogs have compassed me*, and *the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me*. The line that follows is *they pierced my hands and my feet*. The hall is the ring, and the road out of it ends at the nails.
cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.member_sentence: The psalmist is ringed by dogs and an assembly of the wicked, and his hands and feet are pierced.

cards.prose: The first promise in Genesis sets the serpent's seed against the woman's seed: *it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel*. Matthew does not quote it, so this is a reading line on line, but the hall shows that enmity out in the open, and the verse says whose head is bruised in the end.
cards.member_phrase: between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel
cards.member_sentence: The woman's seed will bruise the serpent's head while the serpent bruises his heel, read here beside the soldiers' sport.
cards.flag: A reading line on line, not a stated fulfilment; Matthew does not quote Genesis 3:15.

cards.prose: Genesis names thorns and thistles as what the ground under the curse would bring forth. The soldiers plat thorns into a crown and set it on his head in that hall. Matthew does not point back to Genesis, so we read the two line on line: the thorns of the curse on the ground now lie on his head.
cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.member_sentence: The ground under the curse brings forth thorns and thistles, read beside the crown of thorns.
cards.flag: A reading line on line, not a stated fulfilment; Matthew does not quote Genesis 3:18.

cards.prose: The passers-by in both gospels wag their heads and throw the temple saying at him. Mark has one more sound, *Ah*, a cry of contempt, and the charge shouted from the road is the one the court could not make stand when it went looking for two agreeing witnesses. It has passed from the court to the crowd on the road.
cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.member_sentence: Mark has the passers-by cry Ah and throw the temple saying at him as they wag their heads.

cards.prose: Luke says who joined in: *the rulers also with them derided him*, saying *He saved others; let him save himself*. In Matthew the same words come from the chief priests, scribes and elders, so the rulers' voice is the one behind the wagging heads. Luke has them say *the chosen of Elohim (God)*, using the name of the one they say he is not.
cards.member_phrase: And the people stood beholding. And the rulers also with them derided him, saying, He saved others; let him save himself, if he be Messiah (Christ), the chosen of Elohim (God).
cards.member_sentence: Luke names the rulers among the onlookers, deriding him as one who saved others and cannot save himself.

cards.prose: While the passers-by wag their heads and the rulers sneer, John says who stands near, his mother and her sister and two women named Mary. Matthew sees the women from a distance, *many women were there beholding afar off* (Matthew 27:55), and John sets some of them at the cross itself. The mockers laughed, and these stayed.
cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.member_sentence: John names the women standing by the cross, among them his mother and Mary Magdalene.

cards.prose: The cry Matthew records is the opening line of David's psalm, and the men wagging their heads below him are speaking the lines David wrote for his mockers. Yahusha (Jesus) opens a psalm that does not end at being forsaken; it goes on to *I will declare thy name unto my brethren* (Psalm 22:22), so the cry begins the psalm and does not close it.
cards.member_phrase: why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?
cards.member_sentence: David's opening cry, the line Yahusha (Jesus) takes up, which begins a psalm and does not close it.

cards.prose: David says *in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink*, and Matthew shows it twice: the vinegar mingled with gall offered at Golgotha, which he tasted and would not drink, and the sponge of vinegar lifted on a reed after his cry. The men at the cross are handing him David's cup.
cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.member_sentence: David's gall for meat and vinegar for thirst, the cup the crowd offers him at the cross.

cards.prose: Amos says *in that day* the sun will go down at noon and the earth will be darkened *in the clear day*. Matthew has darkness over all the land from the sixth hour, which is noon, to the ninth, while he hangs there. The darkness is not weather but the day Amos names, with Yahuah (the LORD) behind it.
cards.member_phrase: that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day
cards.member_sentence: Amos has the sun go down at noon in that day, the darkness over the land at the cross.

cards.prose: The people at the cross read helplessness into what they see. Yahusha (Jesus) had already said what it was: *I lay down my life*, and his Father loves him for it, *that I might take it again*. The one they tell to save himself is giving his life, and the giving is something his Father loves in him.
cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.member_sentence: He says his Father loves him because he lays down his life to take it again, not as a man overpowered.

cards.prose: The loud cries in Matthew are what Hebrews describes: in the days of his flesh he sent up *prayers and supplications* with strong crying and tears to the one who could save him from death, and the writer says it was heard. The mockers tell him to save himself; the verse shows him asking the one who could.
cards.member_phrase: when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death
cards.member_sentence: Hebrews says in the days of his flesh he prayed with strong crying and tears to the one able to save him.

cards.prose: John shows the same afternoon from outside the temple: it was *the preparation*, with a Sabbath coming that was *an high day*, and men hurried to have the bodies off the crosses before it. The veil is torn and the day of preparation is still being kept; nothing in either verse treats the Sabbath as finished.
cards.member_phrase: because it was the preparation, that the bodies should not remain upon the cross on the sabbath day, (for that sabbath day was an high day,)
cards.member_sentence: John places the tearing of the veil in the afternoon of the preparation, with a high-day Sabbath close at hand.
cards.flag: The old note points to Zechariah 12:10, which John quotes a few verses later (19:37), not at 19:31; the prose stays with what 19:31 says.

cards.prose: Mark explains the hour Matthew calls only evening: it was *the preparation, that is, the day before the sabbath*. Joseph moves at once, with the Sabbath coming on, and the body is laid in the tomb before it begins. The day was kept even in grief.
cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.member_sentence: Mark says it was the evening of the preparation, the day before the Sabbath, when Joseph came for the body.

cards.prose: Luke gives Joseph's character: *a counsellor; and he was a good man, and a just*. He sat in the very body that condemned Yahusha (Jesus), and Luke says *The same had not consented to the counsel and deed of them* (Luke 23:51). A court is a system, and there was a just man inside it who would not go along.
cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.member_sentence: Luke calls Joseph a counsellor, a good man and a just, who had not consented to the council's deed.

cards.prose: John adds that Joseph was a disciple *secretly for fear of the Yahudim (Jews)*. He was a Yahudi (Jew) himself, so John means the men who held the power, the court that had just put Yahusha (Jesus) to death. The man who had kept quiet goes in to the governor and asks for the body, and Pilate gives it.
cards.member_phrase: Joseph of Arimathaea, being a disciple of Yahusha (Jesus), but secretly for fear of the Yahudim (Jews), besought Pilate
cards.member_sentence: John says Joseph was a disciple in secret and asked Pilate for the body, which Pilate gave him.

cards.prose: Matthew names the man who takes the body: a rich man named Joseph. Isaiah says the servant's grave was *with the rich in his death*, and gives the reason in the same breath: *he had done no violence*, and no deceit was in his mouth. The rich man's tomb is the place the verse expected for one who was innocent though he died among the wicked.
cards.member_phrase: and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth
cards.member_sentence: Isaiah says the servant's grave was with the rich in his death, because he had done no violence.

cards.prose: This chapter ends with the chief priests sealing the stone and setting a watch so that no one could say he was risen. The next chapter has the watch walking back into the city to tell those same chief priests *all the things that were done*. The system that sealed the tomb is the first to hear what happened at it, from its own guards.
cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.member_sentence: Some of the watch come into the city and tell the chief priests all that was done at the tomb.

new_threads.title: Judas, the silver and the potter's field
new_threads.summary_md:
It ain't new. The silver, the potter and the field were in the Torah and the prophets long before Judas carried the money back. Matthew says the priests would not put it in the treasury:

*And the chief priests took the silver pieces, and said, It is not lawful for to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood.* (Matthew 27:6)

The Torah already had a line for such money:

*Thou shalt not bring the hire of a whore, or the price of a dog, into the house of Yahuah Elohayka (the LORD thy God) for any vow: for even both these are abomination unto Yahuah Elohayka (the LORD thy God).* (Deuteronomy 23:18)

Matthew then names Jeremiah the prophet for the thirty pieces and the potter's field. The potter and the bought field are Jeremiah's, and the silver thrown to the potter is in Zechariah, so each text is set down here as it stands:

*So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver.* (Zechariah 11:12)

*And Yahuah (LORD) said unto me, Cast it unto the potter: a goodly price that I was prised at of them.* (Zechariah 11:13)

*Thus saith Yahuah (LORD), Go and get a potter's earthen bottle, and take of the ancients of the people, and of the ancients of the priests;* (Jeremiah 19:1)

David had spoken of the man who turns, and Peter reads him over Judas:

*Let his days be few; and let another take his office.* (Psalm 109:8)

*Men and brethren, this scripture must needs have been fulfilled, which the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit) by the mouth of David spake before concerning Judas, which was guide to them that took Yahusha (Jesus).* (Acts 1:16)

Judas chose his side, and the priests who paid him and then refused the money kept a commandment while the innocent man it paid for was handed over.

new_threads.title: Pilate and Barabbas, the silence and the court
new_threads.summary_md:
It ain't new. Before Pilate asks his question the prophet had already described the man who would stand silent, and the psalm had already described the rulers gathered against him. Matthew says:

*And when he was accused of the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing.* (Matthew 27:12)

*He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.* (Isaiah 53:7)

Pilate himself did not want the death. Matthew says what moved the crowd, and who moved it:

*But the chief priests and elders persuaded the multitude that they should ask Barabbas, and destroy Yahusha (Jesus).* (Matthew 27:20)

Peter later says the same of Pilate, and puts the handing over where it belongs:

*The Elohim (God) of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob, the Elohim (God) of our fathers, hath glorified his Son Yahusha (Jesus); whom ye delivered up, and denied him in the presence of Pilate, when he was determined to let him go.* (Acts 3:13)

Mark and Luke each show the same hearing from another side, as the whole council binds him and leads him to the governor, and John shows the rulers outside the hall, careful not to be defiled before the passover. In every telling the weight sits on the court that owned the proceeding, with a governor who knew it was envy and a crowd the rulers had worked on, and the one before them opens not his mouth.

new_threads.title: The burial and the watch
new_threads.summary_md:
It ain't new. Isaiah had already said where the servant's grave would be, and why:

*And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.* (Isaiah 53:9)

Matthew brings in the man who fits it:

*When the even was come, there came a rich man of Arimathæa, named Joseph, who also himself was Yahusha's (Jesus') disciple:* (Matthew 27:57)

*And laid it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock: and he rolled a great stone to the door of the sepulchre, and departed.* (Matthew 27:60)

Luke says what kind of man he was and where he sat:

*And, behold, there was a man named Joseph, a counsellor; and he was a good man, and a just:* (Luke 23:50)

Mark says what hour it was, with the Sabbath coming on, and John says Joseph had been a disciple in secret. The council had condemned Yahusha (Jesus), and a just man from that same council asked for the body.

Then the court seals what it can:

*So they went, and made the sepulchre sure, sealing the stone, and setting a watch.* (Matthew 27:66)

And the next chapter shows what the sealing brought back to them:

*Now when they were going, behold, some of the watch came into the city, and shewed unto the chief priests all the things that were done.* (Matthew 28:11)

The tomb was a rich man's, the stone was sealed by the rulers, and the first report of what happened there went to the system that sealed it.
